title: LIV Golf Lands Mystery Investor, Players to Become Majority Owners
summary: LIV Golf has found a financial lifeline. CEO Scott O'Neil announced Wednesday that the league has signed an agreement with an unnamed lead investor, approved by the board, to replace the Saudi Arabian Public Investment Fund (PIF), which said in April it would stop funding the venture at the end of 2026. The PIF had sunk a reported $5 billion into LIV since its 2022 launch. The new capital infusion, expected to close in September, comes as the league faced an uncertain future: it canceled its New Orleans event and reportedly nixed its season-ending team championship, with some speculating about possible Chapter 11 bankruptcy. O'Neil said the deal will 'make our players the majority equity holders in LIV Golf, a first for a major global sports league.' He added that more than a dozen other parties have expressed interest in becoming minority investors, creating a 'multipartner model built for long-term stability.' No financial details were disclosed, but Sportico previously reported LIV was seeking $250 million to $350 million. The league plans to return next season with 10 events—five international and five in the U.S. This weekend, LIV is playing at Trump National Golf Club Bedminster in New Jersey. The player-driven ownership model marks a radical shift in professional sports, potentially giving athletes unprecedented control over the league's direction.
why_it_matters: If LIV Golf succeeds with players as majority owners, it could transform how professional sports leagues are structured, giving athletes a much larger say in their own leagues. This model challenges the traditional billionaire-owner setup and could influence other sports, affecting how young people might one day watch, play, or work in professional athletics.

background_read: LIV Golf was launched in 2022 as a rival to the established PGA Tour. It offered huge contracts to star players like Phil Mickelson and introduced a shorter 54-hole format with team competitions. The league was entirely funded by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund (PIF)—the country's sovereign wealth fund, which invests oil revenue globally.

The PIF's involvement sparked controversy. Critics accused Saudi Arabia of 'sportswashing' to improve its image amid human rights concerns. The league spent an estimated $5 billion before the PIF announced it would stop funding LIV by the end of 2026, forcing the league to find new investors or risk collapse.

Chapter 11 bankruptcy, mentioned as a possibility in the article, is a U.S. legal process that allows companies facing financial trouble to restructure and negotiate with creditors. An equity holder owns a percentage of a company—most professional sports teams are owned by wealthy individuals or families, not by the players themselves, making LIV's model a rare experiment in athlete control.

perspectives.description: Supporters argue giving athletes majority ownership is a groundbreaking move that corrects the power imbalance in sports. Players would now have a direct stake in the league's success and a voice in decisions on formats, schedules, and revenue sharing. It could attract top talent tired of traditional structures.

Skeptics note that the lead investor remains unnamed and the deal hasn't closed yet, leaving LIV's future precarious. Canceling events and discussing bankruptcy suggests deep financial trouble. If the new money doesn't materialize or comes with hidden strings, player-owners could end up bearing losses or losing their equity.

The shift from Saudi sovereign wealth to a private investor (and eventually many minority partners) may reduce the 'sportswashing' criticism but introduces new uncertainties. The multipartner model is untested in top-tier global sports; its stability depends on whether enough investors can agree on long-term strategy, especially if the league remains unprofitable.

If LIV's player-ownership model succeeds, other sports leagues might follow, potentially reshaping labor relations and team management across the industry. However, if the league fails, it could discourage similar experiments. The resolution of the PGA Tour-LIV Golf rivalry, and whether a merger eventually happens, will also greatly affect the future of professional golf.
